Local fishermen and lighthouse keepers reported it had completely disappeared by the 1940s.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:3-4)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:0-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:2-18)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-19) Extensive targeted surveys between 1956 and 1986 failed to find any evidence of the Canary Islands oystercatcher surviving, and no sightings have occurred during regular bird censuses of the islands in the 21st century.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:5-10)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-20) The Canary Islands oystercatcher has been considered extinct on the IUCN Red List since 1994.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:112-21)

There were sight records of 3 black oystercatchers from the coast of Senegal in 1970 and 1975 (in the Ziguinchor Region).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:2-18) As the Canary Island oystercatcher was never recorded outside the Canaries archipelago before its likely extinction, these sightings are unlikely to represent this species.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:5-10)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:2-18) Still, no other black species of oystercatcher occurs near Senegal; additionally, melanism is not known in the Eurasian oystercatcher which does winter in the region.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:4-8)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:0-17)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-22) Unconfirmed records from Tenerife – in July 1968 at Puerto de la Cruz, and in 1981 at El Médano – could indicate that a small population persisted on uninhabited islets until the early 1980s.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:2-18)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-iucn-1) Second-hand records from Tenerife also exist for the 19th century.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-23)

Over-harvesting of intertidalshellfish by humans was probably the primary cause of the decline and extinction of the Canary Island oystercatcher.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:2-18) Some authors also implicate predation by rats and cats, as well as direct human hunting and harvesting of eggs.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:0-17)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:6-24) Given the small starting size of the population, museum collecting may have been an important contributing factor once the decline was under way.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:6-24) Unsustainable agricultural practices and deforestation led to widespread desertification by the end of the 19th century, which may have contributed to pressure on intertidal habitats by increasing runoff and further driving harvesting of intertidal invertebrates as a food source to compensate for decreased agricultural productivity.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:2-18)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-25)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-26)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-27)

Eight skins and one egg specimen are known to exist.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:4-8)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-28) Three are kept in the British Museum of Natural History, including both the type specimen (BMNH 1905.12.22.323, a female collected at Jandía, Fuerteventura on April 7, 1888) and the last known individual.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-29)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:7-30)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-31) One is located in the World Museum collected by Edmund Meade-Waldo in La Graciosa, a further two in Manchester Museum, and two more in the Museum Koenig Bonn.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:4-8)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:7-30) The only existing egg specimen is at the State Museum of Zoology, Dresden.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-32)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-33) Four other specimens from historical records have disappeared, including the initial specimens collected in 1829 from La Graciosa by Sabin Berthelot and one shot in April 1852 near Jandía by Carl Bolle.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-34)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-35) Another skin at the Tring Museum collected from The Gambia may represent this species,

but is not universally accepted.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-36)

This chapter synthesizes the information in the conservation assessments of the various oystercatcher species and subspecies. The Canary Island Oystercatcher _Haematopus meadewaldoi_ went extinct in about 1940,leaving 11 surviving oystercatcher species. Between two and five subspecies are recognized for three species of oystercatcher, making a total of 18 surviving taxa (excluding _buturlini_ as a separate subspecies of the Eurasian Oystercatcher).
The volume and quality of information available on the feeding ecology, life history, population size and trends, conservation status and threats, are highly variable between the various (sub)species. Whereas the nominate subspecies ostralegus of the Eurasian Oystercatcher Haematopus ostralegus is the best studied shorebird in the world, hardly any information is available on some other (sub)species.

### Files
All oystercatcher species are long-lived and dependent on coastal habitats during the non-breeding season.Many species and populations are coastal throughout the year, but some populations of some species move inland to breed. Oystercatchers breed on the open ground, making nests and chicks vulnerable to flooding,predation and destruction by human activities. ‘Black’ oystercatcher species are generally found on rocky shores, while ‘pied’ species are more often found on beaches, sandy shores, muddy coasts and estuaries.The current IUCN Red List of Threatened Species (IUCN 2013) only addresses the conservation status of oystercatcher species, not subspecies or subpopulations. Many subspecies have disjunct geographical distributions,so that if the subspecies went extinct, the empty area would not be re-occupied quickly by another subspecies. Furthermore, some subspecies have small population sizes. Indeed, the Chatham Oystercatcher _Haematopus chathamensis_ has been classified as ‘Endangered’ since 1994 because of its small population size. We suggest that the subspecies galapagensis of the American Oystercatcher Haematopus palliatus should be classified as ‘Endangered’ and the subspecies frazari of the American Oystercatcher as ‘Vulnerable’ because of their small population sizes. The subspecies osculans of the Eurasian Oystercatcher should be classified as ‘Near Threatened’. IUCN may wish to consider revising the classification of the American Black Oystercatcher to ‘Near Threatened’ from ‘Least Concern’, but clear declines or fluctuations of population and distribution have not been demonstrated.
Coastal development and human activities in the coastal zone are the most important threat to oystercatcher species around the world under present conditions. Increasing human use of the coastal zone in combination with sea-level rise may well be the greatest threat in the future.

The **Canary Islands oystercatcher**, **Canarian oystercatcher**, or **Canarian black oystercatcher** (_**Haematopus meadewaldoi**_)[[notes 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-2) is an extinctshorebird of uncertain taxonomy endemic to Fuerteventura, Lanzarote, and their offshore islets (Islote de Lobos and the Chinijo Archipelago) in the Canary Islands in Spain. Its population declined sharply beginning in the 1800s due primarily to overharvesting by humans of their shared food sources in the intertidal zone. Since the 1940s, the Canary Islands oystercatcher has been considered to be extinct.
texts.1:
The taxonomic status of the species is uncertain. The Canary Islands oystercatcher was considered a population of the African oystercatcher (_Haematopus moquini_) until David Armitage Bannerman identified it as the unique subspecies _H. m. meadewaldoi_ in 1913.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-3) Work by Philip Hockey in 1982 found the Canary Islands oystercatcher to be distinct enough from the African oystercatcher to be split into its own species.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:3-4) Subsequent analysis of the Canary Islands oystercatcher's mitogenome found its genetic differentiation to fall well within the range observed in the Eurasian oystercatcher (_Haematopus ostralegus_) and proposed that _H. meadewaldoi_ be reclassified as either a melanisticcolour morph or subspecies.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-Senfeld-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:1-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-7) However, other researchers argue based on morphometry that _H. meadewaldoi_ is as distinct from _H. ostralegus_ as other generally accepted species.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:4-8) As of 2025, taxonomies such as the IOC World Bird List and Clements list continue to accept _H. meadewaldoi_ as a distinct species.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:5-10)
19th century illustration
texts.2: The Canary Islands oystercatcher was of similar size as its relatives, the African and Eurasian oystercatchers, at about 43 cm (17 in).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:8-11) It was slightly lighter than the African species, which weighs between 600–800 grams (21–28 oz), with females being heavier than males.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-12) Its bill was 80–86 mm (3.1–3.4 in) long in males and markedly longer in females, around 87–92 mm (3.4–3.6 in). The tarsus measured around 53 mm (2.1 in), and the wings were around 250 mm (9.8 in) long.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:4-8) Its bill was laterally compressed, and with a blunt, lighter tip. The eye was red, with a narrow reddish-orange naked eye ring, and the legs and feet were dark pink with ivory-coloured nails. As usual in oystercatchers, it had no hallux and the second and third toes were connected by a small web.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-13)
texts.3:
The overall appearance of the Canary Islands oystercatcher was extremely similar to the African species, to the extent that even museum specimens are difficult to distinguish except by measurements,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-14) or genetic tests.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-Senfeld-5) Its bill was longer and its wings were shorter than in the African species.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:4-8)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:8-11)_H. meadewaldoi_ had a glossy black colour overall save for the whitish underwing bases of the primary remiges' inner webs, but this may have not been present in worn plumage which also was duller. The distribution did not overlap with the African oystercatcher _H. moquini_, which is not known to occur north of Lobito, Angola at least in modern times, though a specimen in the British Museum from Gambia in 1938 proved to be a vagrant _H. moquini_ on genetic analysis.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-Senfeld-5)
The sexes did not differ in plumage; juvenile birds are unknown but probably had duller bare parts and some greyish-buff fringes to the feathers. The colour of downy young is likewise unknown; these are generally brownish-grey above with dark striping to provide camouflage against predators such as gulls; considering the dark lava rock habitat of this species, they were probably fairly dark overall and had a dusky belly.

### Info
**Pages**
5 – 22
**Published**
26 August 14
**Authors**
Bruno J. Ens, Les G. Underhill

### Files
**Public Files**
*   Full text
This chapter synthesizes the information in the conservation assessments of the various oystercatcher species and subspecies. The Canary Island Oystercatcher _Haematopus meadewaldoi_ went extinct in about 1940,leaving 11 surviving oystercatcher species. Between two and five subspecies are recognized for three species of oystercatcher, making a total of 18 surviving taxa (excluding _buturlini_ as a separate subspecies of the Eurasian Oystercatcher).
The volume and quality of information available on the feeding ecology, life history, population size and trends, conservation status and threats, are highly variable between the various (sub)species. Whereas the nominate subspecies ostralegus of the Eurasian Oystercatcher Haematopus ostralegus is the best studied shorebird in the world, hardly any information is available on some other (sub)species.

### Files
All oystercatcher species are long-lived and dependent on coastal habitats during the non-breeding season.Many species and populations are coastal throughout the year, but some populations of some species move inland to breed. Oystercatchers breed on the open ground, making nests and chicks vulnerable to flooding,predation and destruction by human activities. ‘Black’ oystercatcher species are generally found on rocky shores, while ‘pied’ species are more often found on beaches, sandy shores, muddy coasts and estuaries.The current IUCN Red List of Threatened Species (IUCN 2013) only addresses the conservation status of oystercatcher species, not subspecies or subpopulations. Many subspecies have disjunct geographical distributions,so that if the subspecies went extinct, the empty area would not be re-occupied quickly by another subspecies. Furthermore, some subspecies have small population sizes. Indeed, the Chatham Oystercatcher _Haematopus chathamensis_ has been classified as ‘Endangered’ since 1994 because of its small population size. We suggest that the subspecies galapagensis of the American Oystercatcher Haematopus palliatus should be classified as ‘Endangered’ and the subspecies frazari of the American Oystercatcher as ‘Vulnerable’ because of their small population sizes. The subspecies osculans of the Eurasian Oystercatcher should be classified as ‘Near Threatened’. IUCN may wish to consider revising the classification of the American Black Oystercatcher to ‘Near Threatened’ from ‘Least Concern’, but clear declines or fluctuations of population and distribution have not been demonstrated.
Coastal development and human activities in the coastal zone are the most important threat to oystercatcher species around the world under present conditions. Increasing human use of the coastal zone in combination with sea-level rise may well be the greatest threat in the future.

The **Canary Islands oystercatcher**, **Canarian oystercatcher**, or **Canarian black oystercatcher** (_**Haematopus meadewaldoi**_)[[notes 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-2) is an extinctshorebird of uncertain taxonomy endemic to Fuerteventura, Lanzarote, and their offshore islets (Islote de Lobos and the Chinijo Archipelago) in the Canary Islands in Spain. Its population declined sharply beginning in the 1800s due primarily to overharvesting by humans of their shared food sources in the intertidal zone. Since the 1940s, the Canary Islands oystercatcher has been considered to be extinct.

The taxonomic status of the species is uncertain. The Canary Islands oystercatcher was considered a population of the African oystercatcher (_Haematopus moquini_) until David Armitage Bannerman identified it as the unique subspecies _H. m. meadewaldoi_ in 1913.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-3) Work by Philip Hockey in 1982 found the Canary Islands oystercatcher to be distinct enough from the African oystercatcher to be split into its own species.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:3-4) Subsequent analysis of the Canary Islands oystercatcher's mitogenome found its genetic differentiation to fall well within the range observed in the Eurasian oystercatcher (_Haematopus ostralegus_) and proposed that _H. meadewaldoi_ be reclassified as either a melanisticcolour morph or subspecies.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-Senfeld-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:1-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-7) However, other researchers argue based on morphometry that _H. meadewaldoi_ is as distinct from _H. ostralegus_ as other generally accepted species.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:4-8) As of 2025, taxonomies such as the IOC World Bird List and Clements list continue to accept _H. meadewaldoi_ as a distinct species.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:5-10)
19th century illustration

The Canary Islands oystercatcher was of similar size as its relatives, the African and Eurasian oystercatchers, at about 43 cm (17 in).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:8-11) It was slightly lighter than the African species, which weighs between 600–800 grams (21–28 oz), with females being heavier than males.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-12) Its bill was 80–86 mm (3.1–3.4 in) long in males and markedly longer in females, around 87–92 mm (3.4–3.6 in). The tarsus measured around 53 mm (2.1 in), and the wings were around 250 mm (9.8 in) long.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:4-8) Its bill was laterally compressed, and with a blunt, lighter tip. The eye was red, with a narrow reddish-orange naked eye ring, and the legs and feet were dark pink with ivory-coloured nails. As usual in oystercatchers, it had no hallux and the second and third toes were connected by a small web.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-13)

The overall appearance of the Canary Islands oystercatcher was extremely similar to the African species, to the extent that even museum specimens are difficult to distinguish except by measurements,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-14) or genetic tests.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-Senfeld-5) Its bill was longer and its wings were shorter than in the African species.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:4-8)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-:8-11)_H. meadewaldoi_ had a glossy black colour overall save for the whitish underwing bases of the primary remiges' inner webs, but this may have not been present in worn plumage which also was duller. The distribution did not overlap with the African oystercatcher _H. moquini_, which is not known to occur north of Lobito, Angola at least in modern times, though a specimen in the British Museum from Gambia in 1938 proved to be a vagrant _H. moquini_ on genetic analysis.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-Senfeld-5)
The sexes did not differ in plumage; juvenile birds are unknown but probably had duller bare parts and some greyish-buff fringes to the feathers. The colour of downy young is likewise unknown; these are generally brownish-grey above with dark striping to provide camouflage against predators such as gulls; considering the dark lava rock habitat of this species, they were probably fairly dark overall and had a dusky belly.

The Canary Islands oystercatcher was apparently an all-year resident, and seems to have never bred or even strayed outside the eastern Canaries at least in historic times. Information about its ecology are scant and usually second-hand or inferred from circumstantial information. However, even though conjectural, these informations are consistent as the biology of oystercatchers is not very variable and the species was a conspicuous bird well known to locals. It was called _cuervo marino_ ("sea raven") on Fuerteventura, _grajo de mar_ ("sea chough"[[notes 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands_oystercatcher#cite_note-15)) on Lanzarote, and _corvino_ ("little raven") on Graciosa. In addition, the local name _lapero_ ("limpet-eater") was also used, possibly on Alegranza.
The Canary Islands oystercatcher was in all likelihood a bird of the rocky shore rather than sandy beaches; the latter are scarce on the volcanic Canary Islands, and it might have been driven from them as they were more heavily used by people. What is known about its feeding habits indicates that it had always been less commonly found in beach habitat. As with all oystercatchers, its diet consisted of small molluscs and crustaceans rather than oysters. Especially the limpets_Patella candei_, _Patella piperata_, and _Patella_ cf. _ulyssiponensis_, as well as the African mussel_Perna (perna) picta_ were favoured prey items._[citation needed_]
Its vocalizations were given as repeated _kvirr_ or _kvik-kvikkvik_, and the alarm call_peepe-peepe peepe-peepe_. The birds appear to have been territorial in the breeding season and vagrant, but not occurring in large groups, at other times._[citation needed_]

Like other oystercatchers, this species did not build a nest but laid its eggs in a scrape on the seaside; apparently it chose the most deserted locations such as the mouths of _barrancos_ (erosion gullies); eggs or nests were never recorded by researchers. Its courtship was reported to be peculiar, with two or three males joining in a "dancing" display, presenting themselves to best effect. Once the females had chosen a partner, they remained monogamous, probably for life if the pairing proved successful as in most other species of the genus. The clutch size was undocumented but possibly there was only one egg; groups of three, but not four birds were commonly seen. The eggs can be assumed to have been camouflaged as in its relatives; in the case of this species, they thus were probably rather dark overall, dull brownish grey with plenty of black, dark brown, and dark purplish splotches and scribbles. Egg size was probably about 60 mm ×40 mm (2.4 in ×1.6 in) on average.
The breeding season is also unknown, but from observations of courtship and birds in laying condition, it started around April. Comparison with its relatives suggests that incubation lasted for around 30 days, maybe less, with the chicks taking around 35 days again to fledge. The three-bird groups started to occur on more populated regions in June. Females took probably 3 years to reach sexual maturity and males 4; this species can be assumed to have been long-lived like other oystercatchers, which not infrequently live for 20 or even more than 30 years. Unusually, the birds seem to have moulted after the breeding season; 2 females shot in April had worn plumage.

Species are classified by the IUCN Red List into nine groups: *   Extinct (EX) – beyond reasonable doubt that the species is no longer extant.
*   Extinct in the wild (EW) – survives only in captivity, cultivation and/or outside native range, as presumed after exhaustive surveys.  
*   Critically endangered (CR) – in a particularly and extremely critical state.  
*   Endangered (EN) – very high risk of extinction in the wild, meets any of criteria A to E for Endangered.  
*   Vulnerable (VU) – meets one of the 5 red list criteria and thus considered to be at high risk of unnatural (human-caused) extinction without further human intervention.  
*   Near threatened (NT) – close to being at high risk of extinction in the near future.  
*   Least concern (LC) – unlikely to become extinct in the near future.  
*   Data deficient (DD)  
*   Not evaluated (NE)

The **Pyrenean ibex** (_**Capra pyrenaica pyrenaica**_), Aragonese and Spanish common name _**bucardo**_, Basque common name _**bukardo**_, Catalan common name _**herc**_ and French common name _**bouquetin**_, was one of the four subspecies of the Iberian ibex or Iberian wild goat (_Capra pyrenaica_), a species native to the Iberian Peninsula and immediately adjacent southern France. The Pyrenean ibex occurred in the northeastern part of the species' range in the Cantabrian Mountains and the Pyrenees, in northern Spain and the far south of France. This subspecies was common during the Holocene and Upper Pleistocene, during which their morphology, primarily some skulls, of the Pyrenean ibex evolved to be larger than other subspecies of _Capra pyrenaica_ in southwestern Europe from the same time.

The last Pyrenean ibex died in January 2000, making the subspecies extinct. Other subspecies have survived; the western Spanish or Gredos ibex, and the southeastern Spanish or beceite ibex, while the Portuguese ibex had already become extinct a century earlier. Since the last of the Pyrenean ibex became extinct before scientists could adequately analyse them, the taxonomy of this particular subspecies is controversial.
Following several failed attempts to revive the subspecies through cloning of preserved tissue from the last surviving female, a living specimen was born in July 2003.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2) The cloned Pyrenean ibex was born in Spain through genetic cloning techniques, with the research article published in 2009.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-3) However, she died several minutes after birth of a lung defect.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Theriogenology-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Zimmer-5) The Pyrenean ibex is the first animal to have been brought back from extinction through cloning and also the only one to become extinct twice.
Multiple theories are given regarding the evolution and historical migration of _C. pyrenaica_ into the Iberian Peninsula, and the relationship between the different subspecies.

One possibility is that _C. pyrenaica_ evolved from an ancestor related to _C. caucasica_ from the Middle East, at the beginning of the last glacial period (120–80 ky).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6)_C. pyrenaica_ probably moved from the northern Alps through southern France into the Pyrenees area at the beginning of Magdalenian period about 18 kya. If this is the case, then _C. caucasica praepyrenaica_ may have been more different from the other three ibex species that lived in the Iberian Peninsula than scientists currently know. For example, this would mean that _C. pyrenaica_ (possible migration 18ky) and _C. ibex_ (300 ky earlier migration) would have evolved from different ancestors and been morphologically more different from their separate genes.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6) It is known that all four subspecies lived together in the Upper Pleistocene time, but scientists are unsure of how much genetic exchange could have occurred. The problem with this theory is that genetics suggest that _C. pyrenaica_ and _C. ibex_ may have shared a more common origin, possibly _C. camburgensis_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6)
Many versions of when _C. pyrenaica_ or _C. ibex_ first migrated to and evolved in the Iberian Peninsula are related. _C. pyrenaica_ possibly was already living in the Iberian Peninsula when the ibex began to migrate through the Alps. Genetic evidence also supports the theory that multiple _Capra_ subspecies migrated to the Iberian region around the same time. Hybridisation may have been possible, but the results are not conclusive.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6)

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
[edit]
The Pyrenean ibex had short hair which varied according to seasons. During the summer, its hair was short, and in winter, the hair grew longer and thicker. The hair on the ibex's neck remained long through all seasons. Males and females could be distinguished due to colour, fur, and horn differences. The male was a faded greyish brown during the summer, and marked with black in several places on the body such as the mane, forelegs, and forehead. In the winter, the male transformed from a greyish brown to a dull grey and where the spots were once black, he became dull and faded. The female ibex, though, could be mistaken for a deer since her coat was brown throughout the summer. Unlike the male ibex, females lacked black markings. Young ibex were similar colour to the female for the first year of life.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2)
The male had large, thick horns, curving outwards and backwards, then outwards and downwards, then inwards and upwards. The surface of the horn was ridged, and the ridges developing progressively with age; the number of ridges does not however denote the exact age in years.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2) The female had short, cylindrical horns. Ibex fed on vegetation such as grasses and herbs.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2)
Pyrenean ibex migrated according to seasons. In spring, the ibex would migrate to more elevated parts of mountains where females and males would mate._[citation needed_] In spring, females would normally separate from the males, so they could give birth in more isolated areas. Kids were typically born during May, usually singly. During the winter, the ibex would migrate to valleys that are not covered in snow. These valleys allowed them to eat regardless of the change in season.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2)

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
The species as a whole was often seen in parts of France, Portugal, Spain and Andorra, but not as much in northern areas of the Iberian Peninsula. The Iberian ibex was estimated to have a peak population of 50,000 individuals with more than 50 other subgroups that ranged from the Sierra Nevada to Sierra Morena and Muela de Cortes.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-iucn-1) Many of these subgroups lived in mountainous terrain extending into Spain and Portugal. In areas like Andorra and France in the mainland, the Pyrenean subspecies became extinct first in the northern tip of the Iberian Peninsula. The last remaining Pyrenean ibex were seen in areas of the Middle and Eastern Pyrenees, below 1,200 metres (3,940 ft) altitude. However, in areas of southern France and surrounding areas, ibex were found from 350–925 metres (1,150–3,030 ft) to 1,190–2,240 metres (3,900–7,350 ft).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6)

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
The Pyrenean ibex was abundant until the 14th century and numbers did not dwindle in the region until the mid-19th century.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2) Pyrenean ibex tended to live in rocky habitats with cliffs and trees interspersed with scrub or pine trees. However, smaller patches of rocks in farmland or various areas along the Iberian coast also formed suitable habitat. The ibex was able to thrive well in its environment as long as the appropriate habitat was available, and was able to disperse rapidly and colonise quickly. Pyrenean ibex formed a useful resource for humans, which may have been a cause of their eventual extinction.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-iucn-1) Researchers say that the eventual downfall of the Pyrenean ibex may have been caused by a combination of hunting and that the animal could not compete with the other livestock in the area. However, definite reasons for the extinction of this animal are still unknown.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2)
The subspecies once ranged across the Pyrenees in France and Spain and the surrounding area, including the Basque Country, Navarre, north Aragon, and north Catalonia. A few hundred years ago, they were numerous, but by 1900, their numbers had fallen to fewer than 100. From 1910 onwards, their numbers never rose above 40, and the subspecies was found only in a small part of Ordesa National Park, in Huesca.
Taxidermied specimen of Celia, the endling of her subspecies
The Pyrenean ibex was one of four subspecies of the Iberian ibex. The first to become extinct was the Portuguese ibex (_Capra pyrenaica lusitanica_) in 1892;[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-7) the Pyrenean ibex was the second, with the last individual, a female called Celia, found dead in 2000.

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
In the Middle Ages, Pyrenean ibex were abundant in the Pyrenees region, but decreased rapidly in the 19th and 20th centuries due to hunting pressure. In the second half of the 20th century, only a small population survived in the Ordesa National Park situated in the Spanish Central Pyrenees.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Theriogenology-4)
Competition with domestic and wild ungulates also contributed to the extinction of the Pyrenean ibex. Much of its range was shared with sheep, domestic goats, cattle, and horses, especially in summer when it was in the high mountain pastures. This led to interspecific competition[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-9) and overgrazing, which particularly affected the ibex in dry years. In addition, the introduction of non-native wild ungulate species in areas occupied by the ibex (e.g. fallow deer and mouflon in the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park) increased the grazing pressure, as well as the risk of transmission of both native and exotic diseases.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r4-11)
The last natural Pyrenean ibex, a female named Celia, was found dead on 6 January 2000; she had been killed by a fallen tree. The reason for the subspecies' decline and extinction is not fully understood. Some hypotheses include the inability to compete with other species for food, infections and diseases, and poaching.

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
The Pyrenean ibex became the first taxon ever to become "unextinct" on 30 July 2003,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Tedx-12)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Zimmer-5) when a cloned female ibex was born alive and survived for several minutes, before dying from lung defects.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Theriogenology-4)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r1-13)
Celia, the last ibex, was captured in Ordesa y Monte Perdido National Park in Huesca, Spain; skin biopsies were taken and cryopreserved in nitrogen. She died a year after tissue was harvested from her ear. The American biotechnology company [Advanced Cell Technology, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Cell_Technology,_Inc. "Advanced Cell Technology, Inc.") announced in 2000 that the Spanish government would let them try to clone her from those samples.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-14) ACT intended to work alongside other scientists to clone Celia by nuclear transfer.
It was expected to be easier than the cloning experiment of endangered gaur (_Bos gaurus_), as the reproductive biology of goats is better known and the normal gestation period is only five months. In addition, only certain extinct animals are candidates for cloning because of the need for a suitable proxy surrogate to carry the clone to term. ACT agreed with the government of Aragon that the future cloned Pyrenean ibex would be returned to their original habitat.

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
Celia provided suitable tissue samples for cloning. However, attempts to clone her highlighted a major problem: even if it were possible to produce another healthy Pyrenean ibex, no males were available for the female clone to breed with. To produce a viable population of a previously extinct animal, genetic samples from many individuals would be needed to create genetic diversity in the cloned population.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-15) This is a major obstacle to re-establishing an extinct species population through cloning. One solution could be to cross Celia's clones with males of another subspecies, although the offspring would not be pure Pyrenean ibex. A more ambitious plan would be to remove one X chromosome and add a Y chromosome from another still-existing subspecies, creating a male Pyrenean ibex, but such technology does not yet exist, and it is not known whether this will be feasible at all without irreparable damage to the cell.
Three teams of scientists, two Spanish and one French, are involved in the cloning project. One of the Spanish teams was led by Dr. Jose Folch of Zaragoza, from the Centre of Food Technology and Research of Aragon.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r2-16) The other teams had researchers from the National Research Institute of Agriculture and Food in Madrid.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r1-13)
The project is coordinated by the Food and Agricultural Investigation Service of the Government of Aragon (Spanish: _Servicio de Investigación Agroalimentaria del Gobierno de Aragón_) and by the National Institute of Investigation and Food and Agrarian Technology _(Instituto Nacional de Investigación y Tecnología Agraria y Alimentaria)_. The National Institute of Agrarian Investigation (INRA) of France is also involved in the project.

## Marine fauna also agonizing far from the spotlight
When we think of **endangered animals in Spain**, we usually imagine Mediterranean scrublands or Atlantic forests. However, a good part of our threatened biodiversity lives underwater. In the islands and on our peninsular coasts, many marine species are going through a critical moment, although they rarely occupy headlines.
The Spanish Mediterranean, for example, has lost entire meadows of Posidonia, which are authentic underwater forests where fish, octopuses, and seahorses take refuge. On my visits to Formentera or Cabrera, I was able to verify an evident difference between protected zones and degraded areas. Where the Posidonia remains dense, the water seems cleaner and full of life. When it disappears, the bottom becomes a desert.
Among the **threatened species** of the sea stands the loggerhead turtle, which finds it increasingly difficult to nest due to beaches saturated with artificial light and boats. There is also concern about the state of various species of rays and sharks suffering from historical fishing pressure. They are slow animals, with long reproductive cycles, and any decrease in their numbers is noticed almost immediately.
Even emblematic mammals like the bottlenose dolphin have seen how pollution and underwater noise alter their traditional routes. In the Canary Islands, the sperm whale clashes with a similar problem, because although there is a vibrant ecosystem, it is subjected to increasingly intense maritime traffic. The sound of engines may seem insignificant to us, but in the ocean’s acoustics, it is a maze that confuses, stresses, and sometimes kills.
These examples show that marine conservation needs as much attention as terrestrial conservation. And that to protect the sea, it is not enough to look at the water; we must also watch what we throw into it.

## Other endangered animals
While the struggle for the **Iberian Lynx** or the **Cantabrian Brown Bear** captures public attention and resources, the reality of Spanish biodiversity is that a broad spectrum of less visible fauna also faces limit situations. These groups, which often include **endemic** species with very reduced geographic distributions, fight silently against the degradation of their habitats, pollution, and the pressure of invasive species.
Below is a summary of species with a high degree of threat (CR, EN, VU) in Spain that had not yet been detailed:

**Reptiles**  
**(Lacertids)**La Palma Giant Lizard   
(_Gallotia auaritae_)Critically Endangered   
(CR)Island endemism. Threatened by the **restriction and continuous decline of its habitat** (less than 1 km²), as well as by the reduction of breeding individuals.  
**Reptiles**  
**(Lacertids)**Batuecan Rock Lizard (_Iberolacerta martinezricai_)Critically Endangered   
(CR)Peninsula endemism. Its habitat is restricted to less than 1 km².  
**Amphibians**  
**(Newts)**Montseny Brook Newt   
(_Calotriton arnoldi_)Critically Endangered   
(CR)Endemic species of the peninsula. It is extremely sensitive to the **fragmentation and destruction of its habitat**, climate change, and pollution.  
**Amphibians**  
**(Frogs)**Pyrenean Frog   
(_Rana pyrenaica_)Endangered   
(EN)Endemic species of the peninsula. Affected by **excessive water extraction**, pollution, and emerging diseases.

## Other endangered animals
(National Catalog)Nationally protected species. Its population suffered a **massive mortality** (almost 99%) since 2016 due to a parasitic protozoan.   
_*Its regression is associated with the degradation of Posidonia oceanica meadows._  
**Mollusks (Gastropods)**Ribbed Limpet   
(_Patella ferruginea_)Endangered   
(National Catalog)Endemic to the Western Mediterranean. Its large size makes it an easy prey for collectors, added to the **deterioration of coastal strips**.   
_*Not yet cataloged by the European Red List._  
**Bony Fish**European Eel   
(_Anguilla anguilla_)Critically Endangered   
(CR)Threatened by **overfishing** and **poaching** throughout its development, as well as by the growing demand in Asia for its farming.  
**Insects (Hymenoptera)**_Ammobates dusmeti_ Critically Endangered   
(CR)Endemic species of Spain and southern France, believed extinct in the peninsula. Its current status is unknown following a recent observation.  
**Insects**  
**(Orthoptera)**Gran Canaria Bush Cricket   
(_Acrostira euphorbiae_)Critically Endangered   
(CR)Endemism of the island of La Palma (Canary Islands). Its distribution is less than 20km² with fewer than 200 mature individuals. It is vulnerable to **overgrazing**, logging of its main food source, and **forest fires**.

## Species declared extinct at the national level (RE)
While a titanic battle is waged for the survival of threatened species, it is essential to remember those we have already lost. The IUCN report and the Spanish Catalog of Threatened Species (CEEA) compile a list of animals that have been officially declared extinct at the national level. These cases are a grim reminder that failure in conservation has **irreversible** consequences.
*   **Mediterranean Monk Seal** (_Monachus monachus_): It was an emblematic marine mammal of the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts of Spain. Its local extinction is due to a combination of historical factors: **direct persecution** (due to competition with fishing), **competition for fishing resources**, and the **accelerated degradation of its habitat** (caves and quiet beaches). It was declared **Regionally Extinct (RE)** in Spain, although it still maintains small critical populations in other parts of the Mediterranean and the Atlantic.  
*   **North Atlantic Right Whale** (_Eubalaena glacialis_): This majestic whale, one of the largest species in the world, was declared **Regionally Extinct (RE)** in Spanish waters. Its local extinction was driven almost exclusively by **intensive and uncontrolled hunting** that spanned centuries in the North Atlantic.

## The strategies changing the fate of our fauna
If I have learned anything after more than a decade interviewing biologists, forest agents, and conservation specialists, it is that the recovery of **threatened species** never happens by chance. Behind it, there is always immense human effort, sometimes discreet, sometimes heroic, but always constant.
One of the fundamental pillars has been captive breeding programs. Both the Iberian lynx and the bearded vulture have demonstrated that, if managed with science and patience, this tool can make a difference. The challenge comes when those animals must return to the field. Reintroducing a specimen involves months of preparation and meticulous GPS tracking to understand if it adapts, if it finds food, or if it needs temporary support.
Another key line is habitat restoration. I have walked through old quarries that are today wetlands overflowing with life, and through firebreaks where holm oaks have been planted to recover ecological corridors. These actions may seem small, but they create natural highways for fauna to move without remaining isolated in forest fragments.
Environmental education also marks a turning point. In many mountain villages, neighbors know the rhythms of the countryside better than anyone. When they get involved in projects, the chances of success multiply. I have attended talks where shepherds explained how they coexist with the bear or how they adjust their practices to protect nests of threatened birds. That local wisdom is a resource that cannot be lost.
Many **threatened species** need to move to seek mates, food, or shelter. If they cannot do so because a road splits their world in two, the risk of extinction increases. Green corridors, wildlife crossings, and more coherent territorial planning are pieces still missing in too many regions.

The **Pyrenean ibex** (_**Capra pyrenaica pyrenaica**_), Aragonese and Spanish common name _**bucardo**_, Basque common name _**bukardo**_, Catalan common name _**herc**_ and French common name _**bouquetin**_, was one of the four subspecies of the Iberian ibex or Iberian wild goat (_Capra pyrenaica_), a species native to the Iberian Peninsula and immediately adjacent southern France. The Pyrenean ibex occurred in the northeastern part of the species' range in the Cantabrian Mountains and the Pyrenees, in northern Spain and the far south of France. This subspecies was common during the Holocene and Upper Pleistocene, during which their morphology, primarily some skulls, of the Pyrenean ibex evolved to be larger than other subspecies of _Capra pyrenaica_ in southwestern Europe from the same time.
texts.1:
The last Pyrenean ibex died in January 2000, making the subspecies extinct. Other subspecies have survived; the western Spanish or Gredos ibex, and the southeastern Spanish or beceite ibex, while the Portuguese ibex had already become extinct a century earlier. Since the last of the Pyrenean ibex became extinct before scientists could adequately analyse them, the taxonomy of this particular subspecies is controversial.
Following several failed attempts to revive the subspecies through cloning of preserved tissue from the last surviving female, a living specimen was born in July 2003.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2) The cloned Pyrenean ibex was born in Spain through genetic cloning techniques, with the research article published in 2009.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-3) However, she died several minutes after birth of a lung defect.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Theriogenology-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Zimmer-5) The Pyrenean ibex is the first animal to have been brought back from extinction through cloning and also the only one to become extinct twice.
Multiple theories are given regarding the evolution and historical migration of _C. pyrenaica_ into the Iberian Peninsula, and the relationship between the different subspecies.
texts.2:
One possibility is that _C. pyrenaica_ evolved from an ancestor related to _C. caucasica_ from the Middle East, at the beginning of the last glacial period (120–80 ky).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6)_C. pyrenaica_ probably moved from the northern Alps through southern France into the Pyrenees area at the beginning of Magdalenian period about 18 kya. If this is the case, then _C. caucasica praepyrenaica_ may have been more different from the other three ibex species that lived in the Iberian Peninsula than scientists currently know. For example, this would mean that _C. pyrenaica_ (possible migration 18ky) and _C. ibex_ (300 ky earlier migration) would have evolved from different ancestors and been morphologically more different from their separate genes.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6) It is known that all four subspecies lived together in the Upper Pleistocene time, but scientists are unsure of how much genetic exchange could have occurred. The problem with this theory is that genetics suggest that _C. pyrenaica_ and _C. ibex_ may have shared a more common origin, possibly _C. camburgensis_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6)
Many versions of when _C. pyrenaica_ or _C. ibex_ first migrated to and evolved in the Iberian Peninsula are related. _C. pyrenaica_ possibly was already living in the Iberian Peninsula when the ibex began to migrate through the Alps. Genetic evidence also supports the theory that multiple _Capra_ subspecies migrated to the Iberian region around the same time. Hybridisation may have been possible, but the results are not conclusive.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6)

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
[edit]
The Pyrenean ibex had short hair which varied according to seasons. During the summer, its hair was short, and in winter, the hair grew longer and thicker. The hair on the ibex's neck remained long through all seasons. Males and females could be distinguished due to colour, fur, and horn differences. The male was a faded greyish brown during the summer, and marked with black in several places on the body such as the mane, forelegs, and forehead. In the winter, the male transformed from a greyish brown to a dull grey and where the spots were once black, he became dull and faded. The female ibex, though, could be mistaken for a deer since her coat was brown throughout the summer. Unlike the male ibex, females lacked black markings. Young ibex were similar colour to the female for the first year of life.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2)
The male had large, thick horns, curving outwards and backwards, then outwards and downwards, then inwards and upwards. The surface of the horn was ridged, and the ridges developing progressively with age; the number of ridges does not however denote the exact age in years.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2) The female had short, cylindrical horns. Ibex fed on vegetation such as grasses and herbs.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2)
Pyrenean ibex migrated according to seasons. In spring, the ibex would migrate to more elevated parts of mountains where females and males would mate._[citation needed_] In spring, females would normally separate from the males, so they could give birth in more isolated areas. Kids were typically born during May, usually singly. During the winter, the ibex would migrate to valleys that are not covered in snow. These valleys allowed them to eat regardless of the change in season.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2)

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
The species as a whole was often seen in parts of France, Portugal, Spain and Andorra, but not as much in northern areas of the Iberian Peninsula. The Iberian ibex was estimated to have a peak population of 50,000 individuals with more than 50 other subgroups that ranged from the Sierra Nevada to Sierra Morena and Muela de Cortes.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-iucn-1) Many of these subgroups lived in mountainous terrain extending into Spain and Portugal. In areas like Andorra and France in the mainland, the Pyrenean subspecies became extinct first in the northern tip of the Iberian Peninsula. The last remaining Pyrenean ibex were seen in areas of the Middle and Eastern Pyrenees, below 1,200 metres (3,940 ft) altitude. However, in areas of southern France and surrounding areas, ibex were found from 350–925 metres (1,150–3,030 ft) to 1,190–2,240 metres (3,900–7,350 ft).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6)

One of the Spanish teams was led by Dr. Jose Folch of Zaragoza, from the Centre of Food Technology and Research of Aragon.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r2-16) The other teams had researchers from the National Research Institute of Agriculture and Food in Madrid.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r1-13)
The project is coordinated by the Food and Agricultural Investigation Service of the Government of Aragon (Spanish: _Servicio de Investigación Agroalimentaria del Gobierno de Aragón_) and by the National Institute of Investigation and Food and Agrarian Technology _(Instituto Nacional de Investigación y Tecnología Agraria y Alimentaria)_. The National Institute of Agrarian Investigation (INRA) of France is also involved in the project.

## Marine fauna also agonizing far from the spotlight
When we think of **endangered animals in Spain**, we usually imagine Mediterranean scrublands or Atlantic forests. However, a good part of our threatened biodiversity lives underwater. In the islands and on our peninsular coasts, many marine species are going through a critical moment, although they rarely occupy headlines.
The Spanish Mediterranean, for example, has lost entire meadows of Posidonia, which are authentic underwater forests where fish, octopuses, and seahorses take refuge. On my visits to Formentera or Cabrera, I was able to verify an evident difference between protected zones and degraded areas. Where the Posidonia remains dense, the water seems cleaner and full of life. When it disappears, the bottom becomes a desert.
Among the **threatened species** of the sea stands the loggerhead turtle, which finds it increasingly difficult to nest due to beaches saturated with artificial light and boats. There is also concern about the state of various species of rays and sharks suffering from historical fishing pressure. They are slow animals, with long reproductive cycles, and any decrease in their numbers is noticed almost immediately.
Even emblematic mammals like the bottlenose dolphin have seen how pollution and underwater noise alter their traditional routes. In the Canary Islands, the sperm whale clashes with a similar problem, because although there is a vibrant ecosystem, it is subjected to increasingly intense maritime traffic. The sound of engines may seem insignificant to us, but in the ocean’s acoustics, it is a maze that confuses, stresses, and sometimes kills.
These examples show that marine conservation needs as much attention as terrestrial conservation. And that to protect the sea, it is not enough to look at the water; we must also watch what we throw into it.
texts.9:
## Other endangered animals
While the struggle for the **Iberian Lynx** or the **Cantabrian Brown Bear** captures public attention and resources, the reality of Spanish biodiversity is that a broad spectrum of less visible fauna also faces limit situations. These groups, which often include **endemic** species with very reduced geographic distributions, fight silently against the degradation of their habitats, pollution, and the pressure of invasive species.

texts.11:
## Species declared extinct at the national level (RE)
While a titanic battle is waged for the survival of threatened species, it is essential to remember those we have already lost. The IUCN report and the Spanish Catalog of Threatened Species (CEEA) compile a list of animals that have been officially declared extinct at the national level. These cases are a grim reminder that failure in conservation has **irreversible** consequences.
*   **Mediterranean Monk Seal** (_Monachus monachus_): It was an emblematic marine mammal of the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts of Spain. Its local extinction is due to a combination of historical factors: **direct persecution** (due to competition with fishing), **competition for fishing resources**, and the **accelerated degradation of its habitat** (caves and quiet beaches). It was declared **Regionally Extinct (RE)** in Spain, although it still maintains small critical populations in other parts of the Mediterranean and the Atlantic.  
*   **North Atlantic Right Whale** (_Eubalaena glacialis_): This majestic whale, one of the largest species in the world, was declared **Regionally Extinct (RE)** in Spanish waters. Its local extinction was driven almost exclusively by **intensive and uncontrolled hunting** that spanned centuries in the North Atlantic.
texts.12:
## The strategies changing the fate of our fauna
If I have learned anything after more than a decade interviewing biologists, forest agents, and conservation specialists, it is that the recovery of **threatened species** never happens by chance. Behind it, there is always immense human effort, sometimes discreet, sometimes heroic, but always constant.
One of the fundamental pillars has been captive breeding programs. Both the Iberian lynx and the bearded vulture have demonstrated that, if managed with science and patience, this tool can make a difference. The challenge comes when those animals must return to the field. Reintroducing a specimen involves months of preparation and meticulous GPS tracking to understand if it adapts, if it finds food, or if it needs temporary support.
Another key line is habitat restoration. I have walked through old quarries that are today wetlands overflowing with life, and through firebreaks where holm oaks have been planted to recover ecological corridors. These actions may seem small, but they create natural highways for fauna to move without remaining isolated in forest fragments.
Environmental education also marks a turning point. In many mountain villages, neighbors know the rhythms of the countryside better than anyone. When they get involved in projects, the chances of success multiply. I have attended talks where shepherds explained how they coexist with the bear or how they adjust their practices to protect nests of threatened birds. That local wisdom is a resource that cannot be lost.
Many **threatened species** need to move to seek mates, food, or shelter. If they cannot do so because a road splits their world in two, the risk of extinction increases. Green corridors, wildlife crossings, and more coherent territorial planning are pieces still missing in too many regions.

The **Pyrenean ibex** (_**Capra pyrenaica pyrenaica**_), Aragonese and Spanish common name _**bucardo**_, Basque common name _**bukardo**_, Catalan common name _**herc**_ and French common name _**bouquetin**_, was one of the four subspecies of the Iberian ibex or Iberian wild goat (_Capra pyrenaica_), a species native to the Iberian Peninsula and immediately adjacent southern France. The Pyrenean ibex occurred in the northeastern part of the species' range in the Cantabrian Mountains and the Pyrenees, in northern Spain and the far south of France. This subspecies was common during the Holocene and Upper Pleistocene, during which their morphology, primarily some skulls, of the Pyrenean ibex evolved to be larger than other subspecies of _Capra pyrenaica_ in southwestern Europe from the same time.

The last Pyrenean ibex died in January 2000, making the subspecies extinct. Other subspecies have survived; the western Spanish or Gredos ibex, and the southeastern Spanish or beceite ibex, while the Portuguese ibex had already become extinct a century earlier. Since the last of the Pyrenean ibex became extinct before scientists could adequately analyse them, the taxonomy of this particular subspecies is controversial.
Following several failed attempts to revive the subspecies through cloning of preserved tissue from the last surviving female, a living specimen was born in July 2003.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2) The cloned Pyrenean ibex was born in Spain through genetic cloning techniques, with the research article published in 2009.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-3) However, she died several minutes after birth of a lung defect.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Theriogenology-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Zimmer-5) The Pyrenean ibex is the first animal to have been brought back from extinction through cloning and also the only one to become extinct twice.
Multiple theories are given regarding the evolution and historical migration of _C. pyrenaica_ into the Iberian Peninsula, and the relationship between the different subspecies.

One possibility is that _C. pyrenaica_ evolved from an ancestor related to _C. caucasica_ from the Middle East, at the beginning of the last glacial period (120–80 ky).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6)_C. pyrenaica_ probably moved from the northern Alps through southern France into the Pyrenees area at the beginning of Magdalenian period about 18 kya. If this is the case, then _C. caucasica praepyrenaica_ may have been more different from the other three ibex species that lived in the Iberian Peninsula than scientists currently know. For example, this would mean that _C. pyrenaica_ (possible migration 18ky) and _C. ibex_ (300 ky earlier migration) would have evolved from different ancestors and been morphologically more different from their separate genes.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6) It is known that all four subspecies lived together in the Upper Pleistocene time, but scientists are unsure of how much genetic exchange could have occurred. The problem with this theory is that genetics suggest that _C. pyrenaica_ and _C. ibex_ may have shared a more common origin, possibly _C. camburgensis_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6)
Many versions of when _C. pyrenaica_ or _C. ibex_ first migrated to and evolved in the Iberian Peninsula are related. _C. pyrenaica_ possibly was already living in the Iberian Peninsula when the ibex began to migrate through the Alps. Genetic evidence also supports the theory that multiple _Capra_ subspecies migrated to the Iberian region around the same time. Hybridisation may have been possible, but the results are not conclusive.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6)

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
[edit]
The Pyrenean ibex had short hair which varied according to seasons. During the summer, its hair was short, and in winter, the hair grew longer and thicker. The hair on the ibex's neck remained long through all seasons. Males and females could be distinguished due to colour, fur, and horn differences. The male was a faded greyish brown during the summer, and marked with black in several places on the body such as the mane, forelegs, and forehead. In the winter, the male transformed from a greyish brown to a dull grey and where the spots were once black, he became dull and faded. The female ibex, though, could be mistaken for a deer since her coat was brown throughout the summer. Unlike the male ibex, females lacked black markings. Young ibex were similar colour to the female for the first year of life.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2)
The male had large, thick horns, curving outwards and backwards, then outwards and downwards, then inwards and upwards. The surface of the horn was ridged, and the ridges developing progressively with age; the number of ridges does not however denote the exact age in years.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2) The female had short, cylindrical horns. Ibex fed on vegetation such as grasses and herbs.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2)
Pyrenean ibex migrated according to seasons. In spring, the ibex would migrate to more elevated parts of mountains where females and males would mate._[citation needed_] In spring, females would normally separate from the males, so they could give birth in more isolated areas. Kids were typically born during May, usually singly. During the winter, the ibex would migrate to valleys that are not covered in snow. These valleys allowed them to eat regardless of the change in season.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2)

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
The species as a whole was often seen in parts of France, Portugal, Spain and Andorra, but not as much in northern areas of the Iberian Peninsula. The Iberian ibex was estimated to have a peak population of 50,000 individuals with more than 50 other subgroups that ranged from the Sierra Nevada to Sierra Morena and Muela de Cortes.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-iucn-1) Many of these subgroups lived in mountainous terrain extending into Spain and Portugal. In areas like Andorra and France in the mainland, the Pyrenean subspecies became extinct first in the northern tip of the Iberian Peninsula. The last remaining Pyrenean ibex were seen in areas of the Middle and Eastern Pyrenees, below 1,200 metres (3,940 ft) altitude. However, in areas of southern France and surrounding areas, ibex were found from 350–925 metres (1,150–3,030 ft) to 1,190–2,240 metres (3,900–7,350 ft).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Palevol-6)

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
The Pyrenean ibex was abundant until the 14th century and numbers did not dwindle in the region until the mid-19th century.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2) Pyrenean ibex tended to live in rocky habitats with cliffs and trees interspersed with scrub or pine trees. However, smaller patches of rocks in farmland or various areas along the Iberian coast also formed suitable habitat. The ibex was able to thrive well in its environment as long as the appropriate habitat was available, and was able to disperse rapidly and colonise quickly. Pyrenean ibex formed a useful resource for humans, which may have been a cause of their eventual extinction.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-iucn-1) Researchers say that the eventual downfall of the Pyrenean ibex may have been caused by a combination of hunting and that the animal could not compete with the other livestock in the area. However, definite reasons for the extinction of this animal are still unknown.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r7-2)
The subspecies once ranged across the Pyrenees in France and Spain and the surrounding area, including the Basque Country, Navarre, north Aragon, and north Catalonia. A few hundred years ago, they were numerous, but by 1900, their numbers had fallen to fewer than 100. From 1910 onwards, their numbers never rose above 40, and the subspecies was found only in a small part of Ordesa National Park, in Huesca.
Taxidermied specimen of Celia, the endling of her subspecies
The Pyrenean ibex was one of four subspecies of the Iberian ibex. The first to become extinct was the Portuguese ibex (_Capra pyrenaica lusitanica_) in 1892;[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-7) the Pyrenean ibex was the second, with the last individual, a female called Celia, found dead in 2000.

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
In the Middle Ages, Pyrenean ibex were abundant in the Pyrenees region, but decreased rapidly in the 19th and 20th centuries due to hunting pressure. In the second half of the 20th century, only a small population survived in the Ordesa National Park situated in the Spanish Central Pyrenees.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Theriogenology-4)
Competition with domestic and wild ungulates also contributed to the extinction of the Pyrenean ibex. Much of its range was shared with sheep, domestic goats, cattle, and horses, especially in summer when it was in the high mountain pastures. This led to interspecific competition[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-9) and overgrazing, which particularly affected the ibex in dry years. In addition, the introduction of non-native wild ungulate species in areas occupied by the ibex (e.g. fallow deer and mouflon in the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park) increased the grazing pressure, as well as the risk of transmission of both native and exotic diseases.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r4-11)
The last natural Pyrenean ibex, a female named Celia, was found dead on 6 January 2000; she had been killed by a fallen tree. The reason for the subspecies' decline and extinction is not fully understood. Some hypotheses include the inability to compete with other species for food, infections and diseases, and poaching.

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
The Pyrenean ibex became the first taxon ever to become "unextinct" on 30 July 2003,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Tedx-12)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Zimmer-5) when a cloned female ibex was born alive and survived for several minutes, before dying from lung defects.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-Theriogenology-4)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r1-13)
Celia, the last ibex, was captured in Ordesa y Monte Perdido National Park in Huesca, Spain; skin biopsies were taken and cryopreserved in nitrogen. She died a year after tissue was harvested from her ear. The American biotechnology company [Advanced Cell Technology, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Cell_Technology,_Inc. "Advanced Cell Technology, Inc.") announced in 2000 that the Spanish government would let them try to clone her from those samples.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-14) ACT intended to work alongside other scientists to clone Celia by nuclear transfer.
It was expected to be easier than the cloning experiment of endangered gaur (_Bos gaurus_), as the reproductive biology of goats is better known and the normal gestation period is only five months. In addition, only certain extinct animals are candidates for cloning because of the need for a suitable proxy surrogate to carry the clone to term. ACT agreed with the government of Aragon that the future cloned Pyrenean ibex would be returned to their original habitat.

## Behaviour and physical characteristics
Celia provided suitable tissue samples for cloning. However, attempts to clone her highlighted a major problem: even if it were possible to produce another healthy Pyrenean ibex, no males were available for the female clone to breed with. To produce a viable population of a previously extinct animal, genetic samples from many individuals would be needed to create genetic diversity in the cloned population.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-15) This is a major obstacle to re-establishing an extinct species population through cloning. One solution could be to cross Celia's clones with males of another subspecies, although the offspring would not be pure Pyrenean ibex. A more ambitious plan would be to remove one X chromosome and add a Y chromosome from another still-existing subspecies, creating a male Pyrenean ibex, but such technology does not yet exist, and it is not known whether this will be feasible at all without irreparable damage to the cell.
Three teams of scientists, two Spanish and one French, are involved in the cloning project. One of the Spanish teams was led by Dr. Jose Folch of Zaragoza, from the Centre of Food Technology and Research of Aragon.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r2-16) The other teams had researchers from the National Research Institute of Agriculture and Food in Madrid.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenean_ibex#cite_note-r1-13)
The project is coordinated by the Food and Agricultural Investigation Service of the Government of Aragon (Spanish: _Servicio de Investigación Agroalimentaria del Gobierno de Aragón_) and by the National Institute of Investigation and Food and Agrarian Technology _(Instituto Nacional de Investigación y Tecnología Agraria y Alimentaria)_. The National Institute of Agrarian Investigation (INRA) of France is also involved in the project.
